findings.explanation: The data.template_file data source was replaced with the built-in templatefile() function, but example/examplea/terraform.tf still declares a required_providers entry for hashicorp/template v2.2.0. Terraform will download and initialise this provider on every init even though nothing uses it. The hashicorp/template provider is unmaintained and pinned to a version that predates several security fixes in the Terraform ecosystem.
findings.title: hashicorp/template provider still declared after data.template_file was removed

findings.explanation: The KMS crypto key protecting the bucket declares lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }, but the state bucket itself does not. Terraform state contains all resource outputs including credentials, service account keys, certificates, and database passwords. A mistaken terraform destroy on this workspace would permanently delete the bucket and its contents with no recovery path. No deterministic rule currently checks prevent_destroy on google_storage_bucket.
findings.title: State bucket has no prevent_destroy — a terraform destroy would permanently delete all Terraform state

findings.explanation: HLD_GCP_003 fires because there is no logging block. The checkov:skip=CKV_GCP_62 comment carries no justification. This is not an ordinary bucket — it holds Terraform state containing every secret, key, and credential managed by the workspace. Access logging is the only signal that would reveal an attacker silently exfiltrating state objects. Suppressing it here eliminates the audit trail for the most sensitive GCS bucket in the project.
findings.title: Access logging suppressed on a state bucket with no justification — unauthorized reads of secrets would be invisible

findings.explanation: The local_file resource writes remote_state.tf with no file_permission attribute, so permissions are determined by the process umask — typically 0644 (world-readable) in CI environments. The generated file contains the GCS bucket name for Terraform state. While bucket access still requires GCP authentication, leaking the bucket name in a world-readable file on the runner is unnecessary information disclosure and violates least-privilege hygiene for CI artefacts.
findings.title: local_file.remote_state written with default (potentially world-readable) permissions

suggested_policies.rationale: local_file resources write files to disk with system-default permissions (typically 0644, world-readable) unless file_permission is set explicitly. Files generated by Terraform often contain sensitive configuration such as backend addresses, credentials, or tokens. Requiring file_permission to be set forces the author to make a deliberate choice about who can read the file. coverage_by_type[local_file] is empty — no existing policy covers this.
suggested_policies.yaml:
id: HLD_PROPOSED_001
name: local_file resources must set explicit file permissions
principle: governance
severity: MEDIUM
rationale: |
  The local_file resource writes files to disk using the process umask as the
  default permission, which is typically 0644 (world-readable) in CI/CD
  environments. Terraform-generated files often contain backend addresses,
  credentials, or tokens. Requiring file_permission to be declared forces an
  explicit least-privilege decision rather than silently inheriting a permissive
  default.
remediation: |
  Set file_permission on every local_file resource:

    resource "local_file" "example" {
      content         = "..."
      filename        = "output.txt"
      file_permission = "0600"  # or 0640 if group read is needed
    }
resources:
  local_file:
    path: file_permission
    not_null: true

suggested_policies.rationale: google_storage_bucket has no coverage for lifecycle.prevent_destroy in holden. HLD_TF_041 enforces prevent_destroy on aws_db_instance, aws_dynamodb_table, aws_kms_key, aws_rds_cluster, and google_kms_crypto_key — all resources where accidental deletion causes severe data loss. A GCS bucket used for Terraform state or other persistent data deserves the same protection. Adding google_storage_bucket to HLD_TF_041 (or creating a parallel GCP policy) closes this gap.
suggested_policies.yaml:
id: HLD_PROPOSED_002
name: GCS buckets must enable lifecycle prevent_destroy
principle: backup-and-recovery
severity: HIGH
rationale: |
  A GCS bucket deleted by terraform destroy cannot be recovered if versioning
  and Object Versioning data are lost with it. Buckets used for Terraform state,
  data lakes, or audit logs are especially critical — accidental deletion
  destroys all objects permanently. Setting lifecycle.prevent_destroy = true
  guards against both human error and rogue automation.
remediation: |
  Add a lifecycle block to every google_storage_bucket resource:

    resource "google_storage_bucket" "example" {
      name = "my-bucket"
      # ...
      lifecycle {
        prevent_destroy = true
      }
    }
resources:
  google_storage_bucket:
    path: lifecycle.prevent_destroy
    equals: true
